kernels.definition: A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition and an ordered crystal structure; minerals are identified by physical properties such as hardness, streak, luster, and cleavage.

definitionAnchor.quote: naturally occurring, inorganic, solid at room temperature, regular crystal structure, and defined chemical composition

facts.text: Hardness is measured on the Mohs scale; diamond is a 10 and is about four times harder than corundum, a 9.

anchor.quote: Diamond defines a hardness of 10 and is actually about four times harder than corundum, which is 9

facts.text: Streak is the color of a mineral's powder, and is more reliable than the color of the whole specimen.

anchor.quote: Streak examines the color of a powdered mineral

facts.text: Cleavage is the tendency of a mineral to break along flat planes of weak bonding; minerals without such planes fracture irregularly.

anchor.quote: Cleavage is the tendency of a mineral to break along flat planes of weak bonding

facts.text: Luster describes how a mineral's surface reflects light — metallic, glassy, or dull.

anchor.quote: Luster describes how the mineral looks

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §3.1 What is a mineral; §3.5 Identifying minerals

kernels.definition: Weathering breaks bedrock into sediment in place, while erosion is the transport of that sediment away by water, wind, gravity, or ice.

definitionAnchor.quote: Weathering is a process that turns bedrock into smaller particles, called sediment

facts.text: Erosion is a mechanical process, driven by water, wind, gravity, or ice, that transports sediment.

anchor.quote: Erosion is a mechanical process, usually driven by water, wind, gravity, or ice, which transports sediment

facts.text: Mechanical weathering physically breaks bedrock into smaller pieces without changing its chemistry.

anchor.quote: Mechanical weathering physically breaks bedrock into smaller pieces

facts.text: Chemical weathering dissolves or alters minerals into new substances and dominates in warm, humid environments.

anchor.quote: Chemical weathering is the dominate weathering process in warm, humid environments

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §5.1 Weathering and erosion

kernels.definition: Sedimentary rock forms when sediment is deposited, compacted under burial, and cemented into stone — a process called lithification — and its features record the depositional environment.

definitionAnchor.quote: Deposition happens when friction and gravity overcome the forces driving sediment transport

facts.text: Compaction occurs as more material accumulates on top, squeezing the grains together.

anchor.quote: Compaction occurs when material continues to accumulate on top of the sediment layer

facts.text: Cementation glues the grains together with minerals; compaction and cementation together are lithification.

anchor.quote: Cementation is the process of cementing minerals coating the sediment grains and gluing them together

facts.text: Clastic (detrital) sedimentary rocks are made of pieces of preexisting weathered rock.

anchor.quote: Detrital or clastic sedimentary rocks consist of preexisting sediment pieces that comes from weathered bedrock

facts.text: The features of a sedimentary rock are read to reconstruct its original depositional environment.

anchor.quote: to understand the original depositional environment

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §5.3 Sedimentary rocks

kernels.definition: Metamorphic rock forms when heat, pressure, and fluids change a preexisting parent rock (the protolith) in the solid state, without melting it.

definitionAnchor.quote: Metamorphic rocks are created when heat, pressure, and/or fluids change preexisting rocks

facts.text: Metamorphism changes a solid rock's composition and texture without the mineral crystals melting.

anchor.quote: Metamorphism occurs when solid rock changes composition and/or texture without mineral crystals melting

facts.text: The starting rock that undergoes metamorphism is called the parent rock, or protolith.

anchor.quote: are called the parent rock, or protolith

facts.text: Directed stress aligns mineral crystals into planes, producing foliation.

anchor.quote: Foliation is a term used that describes minerals lined up in planes

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §6.1 Metamorphism and metamorphic rocks

kernels.definition: The rock cycle describes how Earth's three rock families — igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic — form and continually transform into one another through geologic processes.

definitionAnchor.quote: the process of changing rocks on Earth into different forms, namely igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic

facts.text: The rock cycle describes the major Earth materials, the processes that form them, and how they relate to each other.

anchor.quote: describes the major materials that comprise the Earth, the processes that form them, and how they relate to each other

facts.text: Igneous rock forms when liquid rock freezes solid; lithified sediment becomes sedimentary rock; pre-existing rock can transform into metamorphic rock.

anchor.quote: Igneous rock is formed when liquid rock freezes into a solid rock

facts.text: If conditions melt the rocks into magma, the cycle begins anew with new igneous rocks.

anchor.quote: the rock cycle begins anew with the creation of new rocks

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §4 The rock cycle

kernels.definition: Geologic time spans the roughly 4.5-billion-year history of Earth; relative dating orders events by which is older or younger, while absolute dating assigns numerical ages in years.

definitionAnchor.quote: Relative dating is the process of determining if one rock or geologic event is older or younger than another, without knowing their specific ages

facts.text: Absolute (numerical) dating assigns specific ages in years to mineral grains within a rock.

anchor.quote: Absolute dating assigns specific time units, in this case years, to mineral grains within a rock

facts.text: By the principle of superposition, in an undisturbed sequence the bottom layers are oldest and the upper layers younger.

anchor.quote: the layers on the bottom are the oldest, and the layers above them are younger

facts.text: By original horizontality, sediments and lava flows are laid down horizontally, so tilted layers were disturbed after deposition.

anchor.quote: are originally laid down horizontally

facts.text: The Earth is about 4.54 billion years old, and this vastness of geologic time allowed life to evolve.

anchor.quote: The current estimate for the age of the Earth is 4.54 billion years

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §7.1 Relative dating and geologic time

mcItems.q: A student scratches a dark, shiny specimen and sees a white powdery mark. Which property is most useful for identifying the mineral from that result?
mcItems.ex: Streak is the color of a mineral’s powder, so it can be more reliable than the color of the whole specimen. A common misconception is to treat surface shine or specimen color as the main clue, but those describe luster and appearance rather than the powder color used for this test.

mcItems.q: A mineral sample breaks into thin, flat sheets along repeated smooth surfaces. Which description best matches that behavior?
mcItems.ex: Cleavage is the tendency to break along flat planes of weak bonding. The most plausible misconception is to call any breakage a fracture, but fracture is irregular breakage when no such planes are present.

keyTerms.df: The powder color left when a mineral is rubbed on a plate.
keyTerms.eg: A dark specimen may leave a white streak, which helps identify it more reliably than surface color.
keyTerms.mi: Assuming the streak always matches the outside color of the mineral.
keyTerms.cx: The powder can differ from the visible specimen color, so streak is often a better clue for identification.

keyTerms.df: A break pattern formed when a mineral splits along flat surfaces of weak bonding.
keyTerms.eg: A mineral that splits into smooth, flat sheets shows cleavage.
keyTerms.mi: Thinking every mineral that breaks has cleavage.
keyTerms.cx: Minerals without aligned weak planes break irregularly by fracture instead of cleavage.

mcItems.q: A cliff face slowly cracks and crumbles, and the broken pieces stay at the base of the slope. Which process is shown?
mcItems.ex: Mechanical weathering fits because the bedrock is broken into smaller pieces where it is; the common mistake is to call any breakdown or movement “erosion,” but erosion requires transport away of the sediment.

mcItems.q: After a storm, loose grains from a hillside are carried into a stream and moved downstream. What process is happening?
mcItems.ex: Erosion by water is correct because the sediment is being transported away; the plausible misconception is to focus on the grains themselves and label the whole scene as weathering, which would only fit if the material were being broken down in place.

mcItems.q: A student studies a sandstone layer and wants to explain how it became stone. Which process best describes its formation?
op: Sediment is deposited, then compacted and cemented into rock
Melt cools slowly underground until crystals interlock
Existing rock is changed by heat and pressure alone
Minerals dissolve completely and leave a hollow bed
mcItems.ex: Sedimentary rock forms after deposition, burial compaction, and mineral cementation; the common misconception is to confuse this with igneous cooling or metamorphic change.

mcItems.q: A field team uses ripple marks and grain features in a sandstone bed to infer where it formed. What are they using those features for?
op: Measuring the amount of compaction after burial
Identifying the rock as clastic from weathered pieces
Proving the rock formed by cementation alone
mcItems.ex: Those features are read to reconstruct the depositional environment; the misconception is that such features mainly reveal burial compaction rather than the setting of deposition.

keyTerms.df: The burial process that turns loose sediment into solid rock by compaction and cementation.
keyTerms.eg: Mud settles in a basin, is buried by more sediment, and becomes shale-like rock after grains are squeezed together and glued by minerals.
keyTerms.mi: It means only chemical cement is added.
keyTerms.cx: Compaction and cementation together make lithification, so pressure and mineral glue both matter.

keyTerms.df: A sedimentary rock built from fragments of older weathered rock.
keyTerms.eg: Sandstone made from sand-sized bits eroded from preexisting rocks.
keyTerms.mi: It must form from dissolved minerals that crystallize directly from water.
keyTerms.cx: Clastic rocks are fragmental; they come from pieces of earlier rocks rather than direct chemical precipitation.

mcItems.q: A clay-rich shale is buried deep enough to be altered by heat, pressure, and fluids, but it never melts. What best describes the change it undergoes?
op: Breakdown into sediment by surface weathering
Fusion into a magma that cools later
Fragmentation into rounded particles by transport
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is solid-state transformation because metamorphism changes an existing rock without melting it. A common misconception is to treat any deep rock change as melting into magma, but that would require melting, which is not part of metamorphism.

mcItems.q: In a metamorphic outcrop, some mineral crystals are arranged in parallel layers after strong directional pressure. Which feature does that alignment produce?
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is foliation because directed stress aligns mineral crystals into planes. A plausible misconception is to confuse this with sedimentary bedding, but bedding forms during deposition rather than from stress-aligned minerals.

keyTerms.df: Change in a solid rock caused by heat, pressure, and fluids without melting.
keyTerms.eg: A buried shale becoming a metamorphic rock while remaining solid.
keyTerms.mi: It requires the rock to melt first.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that the mineral crystals stay solid during the change.

keyTerms.df: The original parent rock that later undergoes metamorphic change.
keyTerms.eg: A limestone that serves as the starting rock before metamorphism alters it.
keyTerms.mi: It is the mineral pattern created after metamorphism.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that it names the starting rock, not the transformed one.

mcItems.q: A geology student compares two rock layers in an undisturbed outcrop and needs the older layer without assigning a calendar age. Which approach fits best?
op: Use relative dating to rank the layers
Use absolute dating to rank the layers
Use original horizontality to rank the layers
Use geologic time to rank the layers
mcItems.ex: Relative dating is the correct choice because it determines whether one layer is older or younger than another. Absolute dating is the common misconception here because it gives numerical ages in years rather than just an order.

mcItems.q: In a road cut, the sedimentary beds are clearly tilted. What is the best interpretation of that tilt?
op: They were laid down already tilted
They are the youngest beds exposed
They are older than Earth itself
mcItems.ex: The tilt indicates the beds were originally deposited horizontally and were disturbed afterward. A common misconception is that tilted layers must have been deposited that way, but original horizontality says otherwise.

keyTerms.df: A way to place events in older-to-younger order rather than give a numerical age.

keyTerms.mi: It always provides the exact number of years for a rock.
keyTerms.cx: Relative dating tells sequence; absolute dating gives numerical ages.

keyTerms.df: A rule stating that, in an undisturbed stack of layers, lower beds formed before higher ones.
keyTerms.eg: In a flat, undisturbed sedimentary sequence, the bottom bed is the oldest.
keyTerms.mi: The top layer is always the oldest because it is easiest to see.
keyTerms.cx: That is reversed for undisturbed layers; younger layers are on top.

mcItems.q: A student scratches a dark, shiny specimen and sees a white powdery mark. Which property is most useful for identifying the mineral from that result?
mcItems.ex: Streak is the color of a mineral’s powder, so it can be more reliable than the color of the whole specimen. A common misconception is to treat surface shine or specimen color as the main clue, but those describe luster and appearance rather than the powder color used for this test.

mcItems.q: A mineral sample breaks into thin, flat sheets along repeated smooth surfaces. Which description best matches that behavior?
mcItems.ex: Cleavage is the tendency to break along flat planes of weak bonding. The most plausible misconception is to call any breakage a fracture, but fracture is irregular breakage when no such planes are present.

keyTerms.df: The powder color left when a mineral is rubbed on a plate.
keyTerms.eg: A dark specimen may leave a white streak, which helps identify it more reliably than surface color.
keyTerms.mi: Assuming the streak always matches the outside color of the mineral.
keyTerms.cx: The powder can differ from the visible specimen color, so streak is often a better clue for identification.

keyTerms.df: A break pattern formed when a mineral splits along flat surfaces of weak bonding.
keyTerms.eg: A mineral that splits into smooth, flat sheets shows cleavage.
keyTerms.mi: Thinking every mineral that breaks has cleavage.
keyTerms.cx: Minerals without aligned weak planes break irregularly by fracture instead of cleavage.

mcItems.q: A cliff face slowly cracks and crumbles, and the broken pieces stay at the base of the slope. Which process is shown?
mcItems.ex: Mechanical weathering fits because the bedrock is broken into smaller pieces where it is; the common mistake is to call any breakdown or movement “erosion,” but erosion requires transport away of the sediment.

mcItems.q: After a storm, loose grains from a hillside are carried into a stream and moved downstream. What process is happening?
mcItems.ex: Erosion by water is correct because the sediment is being transported away; the plausible misconception is to focus on the grains themselves and label the whole scene as weathering, which would only fit if the material were being broken down in place.

keyTerms.df: The breakdown of bedrock into sediment where the rock remains.
keyTerms.eg: A granite outcrop that crumbles into loose sand at the base of the slope.
keyTerms.mi: It means sediment is carried away by a moving agent.
keyTerms.cx: That description is erosion; weathering happens before transport and leaves the material in place.

keyTerms.df: The transport of sediment away by water, wind, gravity, or ice.
keyTerms.eg: Rainwater moving soil and sand from a slope into a stream channel.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same as breaking rock into smaller pieces.
keyTerms.cx: Breaking rock in place is weathering; erosion begins when the sediment is moved.

mcItems.q: A student studies a sandstone layer and wants to explain how it became stone. Which process best describes its formation?
op: Sediment is deposited, then compacted and cemented into rock
Melt cools slowly underground until crystals interlock
Existing rock is changed by heat and pressure alone
Minerals dissolve completely and leave a hollow bed
mcItems.ex: Sedimentary rock forms after deposition, burial compaction, and mineral cementation; the common misconception is to confuse this with igneous cooling or metamorphic change.

mcItems.q: A field team uses ripple marks and grain features in a sandstone bed to infer where it formed. What are they using those features for?
op: Measuring the amount of compaction after burial
Identifying the rock as clastic from weathered pieces
Proving the rock formed by cementation alone
mcItems.ex: Those features are read to reconstruct the depositional environment; the misconception is that such features mainly reveal burial compaction rather than the setting of deposition.

keyTerms.df: The burial process that turns loose sediment into solid rock by compaction and cementation.
keyTerms.eg: Mud settles in a basin, is buried by more sediment, and becomes shale-like rock after grains are squeezed together and glued by minerals.
keyTerms.mi: It means only chemical cement is added.
keyTerms.cx: Compaction and cementation together make lithification, so pressure and mineral glue both matter.

keyTerms.df: A sedimentary rock built from fragments of older weathered rock.
keyTerms.eg: Sandstone made from sand-sized bits eroded from preexisting rocks.
keyTerms.mi: It must form from dissolved minerals that crystallize directly from water.
keyTerms.cx: Clastic rocks are fragmental; they come from pieces of earlier rocks rather than direct chemical precipitation.

mcItems.q: A clay-rich shale is buried deep enough to be altered by heat, pressure, and fluids, but it never melts. What best describes the change it undergoes?
op: Breakdown into sediment by surface weathering
Fusion into a magma that cools later
Fragmentation into rounded particles by transport
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is solid-state transformation because metamorphism changes an existing rock without melting it. A common misconception is to treat any deep rock change as melting into magma, but that would require melting, which is not part of metamorphism.

mcItems.q: In a metamorphic outcrop, some mineral crystals are arranged in parallel layers after strong directional pressure. Which feature does that alignment produce?
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is foliation because directed stress aligns mineral crystals into planes. A plausible misconception is to confuse this with sedimentary bedding, but bedding forms during deposition rather than from stress-aligned minerals.

keyTerms.df: Change in a solid rock caused by heat, pressure, and fluids without melting.
keyTerms.eg: A buried shale becoming a metamorphic rock while remaining solid.
keyTerms.mi: It requires the rock to melt first.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that the mineral crystals stay solid during the change.

keyTerms.df: The original parent rock that later undergoes metamorphic change.
keyTerms.eg: A limestone that serves as the starting rock before metamorphism alters it.
keyTerms.mi: It is the mineral pattern created after metamorphism.
keyTerms.cx: The correction is that it names the starting rock, not the transformed one.

mcItems.q: A student heats a buried sedimentary rock until minerals recrystallize without melting. Which rock family best fits the product?
mcItems.ex: The best choice is metamorphic rock because pre-existing rock can transform into metamorphic rock. A common misconception is to call any altered rock igneous, but igneous rock requires liquid rock to freeze solid; here, the rock changed without melting.

mcItems.q: After a rock melts, the geologic cycle can start over when the molten material cools and hardens. What new rock family forms first?
mcItems.ex: Igneous rock is correct because liquid rock freezes solid to form igneous rock. A plausible misconception is to choose sedimentary rock, but sedimentary rock forms when sediment is lithified, not when magma cools.

keyTerms.mi: It is just a sequence of rock names.
keyTerms.cx: The cycle links igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks through geologic processes and can begin again if rocks melt into magma.
